Declare the catalog once, at module level, with `createGenerativeUI`:
A component of the catalog is a React Native component. It renders native views, and a slot arrives as React nodes:
import { Image, StyleSheet, Text, View } from "react-native";
function ProductGrid({ title, children }: GenerativeUIComponentProps<typeof shopUI, "ProductGrid">) {
function ProductCard({ name, price, imageUrl }: GenerativeUIComponentProps<typeof shopUI, "ProductCard">) {
description: "A grid of products. Put the ids of ProductCard components in children.",
description: "One product. Copy every value from a product of a tool result.",
props: z.object({ name: z.string(), price: z.number(), imageUrl: z.string() }),
// A fixed width, not a percentage: when the agent sends an `accessibility`
// envelope, the card sits in a wrapper View, and a percentage would resolve
// against that wrapper rather than the grid (see below).
// Margins rather than `gap`, which needs React Native 0.71.
// The Android emulator reaches your machine at 10.0.2.2, not localhost.

`ShopScreen` is your own screen. It shows the surfaces with `GenerativeUIActivity`, in a message list like the `ChatScreen` of [Try it](/ms-agent-harness-dotnet/generative-ui/components#try-it), or with `GenerativeUISurface` in a named area of the screen.
Write the binding in camelCase. Vue does not give `:generative-ui` to the provider.
The `id` names the catalog. Use a versioned id, for example `acme/shop@1`.
- `description`: what the component is and when to use it. The agent reads it, so be specific.
- `props`: the schema of the props that the agent sets.
- `slots`: props that hold child components. `"single"` takes one child, and `"multiple"` takes a list.

- A child reference inside the props schema: mark a prop with `child()` or `childList()` from `@copilotkit/react-core/v2/generative-ui` (in Angular, from `@copilotkit/angular/generative-ui`), anywhere in the schema, for example `tabs: z.array(z.object({ title: z.string(), child: child() }))`. The engine renders the referenced components and your component receives them in place of the ids, as React nodes or as Angular `GenerativeUIChildren` handles. This is how A2UI 1.0 marks references (`ComponentId`, `ChildList`); `slots` stays for the plain top-level case.

- A child reference inside the props schema: mark a prop with `child()` or `childList()` from `@copilotkit/react-core/v2/generative-ui` (in Angular, from `@copilotkit/angular/generative-ui`; on React Native, from `@copilotkit/react-native/generative-ui`; in Vue, from `@copilotkit/vue/v2/generative-ui`), anywhere in the schema, for example `tabs: z.array(z.object({ title: z.string(), child: child() }))`. The engine renders the referenced components and your component receives them in place of the ids, as React nodes, as Angular `GenerativeUIChildren` handles, or as Vue `VNode`s that you render with `<component :is>`. This is how A2UI 1.0 marks references (`ComponentId`, `ChildList`); `slots` stays for the plain top-level case. `child()` and `childList()` return zod 3 schemas, so write a schema that uses them with zod 3: a zod 4 `z.object` that holds one throws when the catalog module loads ("expected a Zod schema"). With zod `^3.25` installed, `import { z } from "zod"` is zod 3; with zod 4, import it from `"zod/v3"`. The React Native setup installs zod 3.
- `events`, `bind`, and `writable`: actions, app state, and inputs. See [Connect app state and actions](/ms-agent-harness-dotnet/generative-ui/components/state-and-actions).

Next to `id` and `component`, every component the agent writes may carry the A2UI 1.0 envelope: `catalogId` (must be the id of your UI), `metadata` (`{ "extensions": { ... } }`, kept for your own tooling) and `accessibility` (`label`, `description`, `live`, `hidden`; `label`, `description` and `hidden` may be bindings or function values). The engine resolves `accessibility` and keeps all three out of your props. `hidden` and `live` apply to every component: the engine wraps the component in an element with `aria-hidden` and `aria-live`. A `label` or a `description` needs an element with a role, so the standard components set them on their root or on their control. In your own component, call `useGenerativeUIAccessibility()` and spread the result on the root element, or bind the result of `injectGenerativeUIAccessibility()` to the host in Angular. A component that must not be wrapped (a table row or cell) declares `accessibility: "self"` and applies the attributes itself.

Next to `id` and `component`, every component the agent writes may carry the A2UI 1.0 envelope: `catalogId` (must be the id of your UI), `metadata` (`{ "extensions": { ... } }`, kept for your own tooling) and `accessibility` (`label`, `description`, `live`, `hidden`; `label`, `description` and `hidden` may be bindings or function values). The engine resolves `accessibility` and keeps all three out of your props. `hidden` and `live` apply to every component: when the agent sends an `accessibility` envelope for a component, the engine wraps it in an element with `aria-hidden` and `aria-live`. A component sent without an envelope gets no wrapper. A `label` or a `description` needs an element with a role, so the standard components set them on their root or on their control. In your own component, call `useGenerativeUIAccessibility()` and spread the result on the root element, or bind the result of `injectGenerativeUIAccessibility()` to the host in Angular. In Vue, put `v-bind` with the result on the root element. On React Native, the wrapper is a real `View` that applies `hidden` and `live` (a live region is announced on Android only; on iOS, announce a change with `AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility`). It never applies `label` or `description`: on iOS a label on a view that is not an accessibility element names nothing, and making the wrapper one would merge every control inside it. It cannot be made layout-transparent, and it becomes the flex item of the parent: a component sized or aligned against its parent (`flex` or `flexGrow` along the parent's main axis, `alignSelf` across it, or a percentage size) resolves against the wrapper instead, so it no longer fills the parent or lines up in it. That is why the `ProductCard` above has a fixed width. A component that needs that sizing declares `accessibility: "self"`, which removes the wrapper, and must then apply `hidden` and `live` itself: set `aria-hidden` and `aria-live` from `useGenerativeUIAccessibility()` on its root view (React Native 0.71+ reads them), or map them to `accessibilityElementsHidden`, `importantForAccessibility` and `accessibilityLiveRegion`. Spreading the whole result works on 0.71+, but it also passes `aria-description`, which React Native has no prop for and ignores. With or without the wrapper, a component that needs a name or a hint reads `aria-label` and `aria-description` from `useGenerativeUIAccessibility()` and sets them on a view of its own that is an accessibility element (`accessible`), for example as `accessibilityLabel` and `accessibilityHint`. A component that must not be wrapped (a table row or cell) declares `accessibility: "self"` and applies the attributes itself.
`GenerativeUIComponentProps<typeof ui, "Name">` gives a component the exact props that the renderer passes. It reads them from the schema, so the component and the catalog cannot drift apart:
props.color; // type error: not a prop of ProductCard
A function component can read its props from its own catalog:
props.color; // type error: not a prop of ProductCard

> Move an app from the a2ui renderer to components and surfaces: the provider, the catalog, the operations, and what the agent receives.

The `a2ui` provider option and `@copilotkit/a2ui-renderer` render A2UI v0.9: you build a catalog with `createCatalog`, and the agent streams a fixed or a generated schema into it. Components and surfaces is the A2UI 1.0 engine. The idea is the same: the agent writes operations, and the browser renders your components. The engine adds typed catalogs, the [standard catalog](/generative-ui/components/standard-catalog), areas of the page as targets, two transports, dynamic values that compute in the browser, and functions the agent can call. This page maps one to the other.

The `a2ui` provider option and `@copilotkit/a2ui-renderer` render A2UI v0.9 by default, with explicit A2UI 1.0 support in React: you build a catalog with `createCatalog`, and the agent streams a fixed or a generated schema into it. Components and surfaces is a separate A2UI 1.0 engine. The idea is the same: the agent writes operations, and the browser renders your components. The engine adds typed catalogs, the [standard catalog](/generative-ui/components/standard-catalog), areas of the page as targets, two transports, dynamic values that compute in the browser, and functions the agent can call. You want the agent to answer with tables, charts, and forms today, not after you build a component library. `standardUI` is a catalog of 69 ready-made components that the agent already knows how to use. The 18 components of the A2UI 1.0 basic catalog are in it under their A2UI names and props (`Image.url`, `CheckBox.value`, `Row.justify: "spaceBetween"`, `weight` for flex-grow); the rest extend the catalog.

Build a catalog of your own native components with `createGenerativeUI`; see [Catalogs](/ms-agent-harness-dotnet/generative-ui/components/catalogs) and [Generative UI with your own components](/ms-agent-harness-dotnet/react-native#generative-ui-with-your-own-components).

- **`Video` takes any URL.** A video file plays in the native player, with `captions` as WebVTT tracks; a YouTube link shows a poster until the user presses play, then loads the privacy-enhanced embed. A page on another video site (Vimeo, Loom, TikTok, …) and a file that fails to load show a link card instead of a dead player. YouTube is the only provider that embeds; to embed another one, [replace the component](#replace-a-component). `Tabs` takes `tabs: [{ "title", "child" }]` with the id of each panel.
- **Inputs keep what users type.** When the agent binds an input to a value, what the user types stays. A later agent update cannot write over it.
- **`Button` and `Pressable` can act in the browser.** `href` opens a URL, and `Button` with `copy` copies text, with no message to the agent.

lines.text: When the user clicks, the click becomes a visible user message, and the agent answers it. The agent can also choose the text of that message (its `userMessage`), for example "Show me the Team plan".

The result of such an event says whether the click was sent, not whether the agent's run worked. It is `ok: false` when it was not sent, for example with the code `agent_busy` while the agent is already running. Otherwise it is `ok: true` once the run that the click started has ended, also when that run failed: a failed run does not throw, and its error goes to the `onError` subscribers of the CopilotKit core, such as the `onError` of `CopilotKitProvider`. Its user message stays in the chat. To show that error next to your chat, subscribe to the core with `copilotkit.subscribe({ onError })` and match `context.agentId`, as the `runTurn` helper of the [React Native guide](/ms-agent-harness-dotnet/react-native#render-surfaces-in-your-message-list) does.

The run that the click starts also carries the structured A2UI 1.0 action message, in `forwardedProps.copilotkit.ui.metadata.extensions.copilotkit_action`: `{ "version": "1.0", "action": { "name": "choose", "surfaceId": "plans", "sourceComponentId": "team-button", "timestamp": "2026-10-20T10:00:00.000Z", "userMessage": "Show me the Team plan", "context": { "plan": "team" } } }`. An agent that wants the structured event reads it from there instead of parsing the message; `envelopeToManifest` from `@copilotkit/shared` gives it back as `action`.

A prop can be a function value as well as a literal or a binding, at any depth: `{ "@call": "formatCurrency", "args": { "value": { "@path": "/total" }, "currency": "EUR" } }`. It recomputes when the data it reads changes, with no round trip to the agent. The functions of the A2UI 1.0 basic catalog are built in: `formatString` (with `${/path}` and `${fn(arg: value)}` interpolation), `formatNumber`, `formatCurrency`, `formatDate`, `pluralize`, `and`, `or`, `not`, the validators `required`, `regex`, `length`, `numeric` and `email`, `@index` in a template, and `openUrl`, which runs only as the `functionCall` of an event.

The functions of the A2UI 1.0 basic catalog are built in: `formatString` (with `${/path}` and `${fn(arg: value)}` interpolation), `formatNumber`, `formatCurrency`, `formatDate`, `pluralize`, `and`, `or`, `not`, the validators `required`, `regex`, `length`, `numeric` and `email`, `@index` in a template, and `openUrl`, which runs only as the `functionCall` of an event and opens only `http` and `https` URLs, in a new tab.

A2UI 1.0 has no arithmetic, so CopilotKit adds two catalog functions. `calc` evaluates an expression over named args: `{ "@call": "calc", "args": { "expression": "seats * 29 * (annual ? 0.8 : 1)", "seats": { "@path": "/seats" }, "annual": { "@path": "/annual" } } }`, with `+ - * / %`, `x ^ y` (power), comparisons, `&& || !`, `?:`, `min`, `max`, `round`, `floor`, `ceil`, `abs`, `pow`, `sqrt`, `exp`, `ln`, `log10`, the constants `pi` and `e`, and text concatenation. `series` builds a list of `count` items from an item template with `${...}` expressions over a loop variable, for chart data. Both appear to the model as regular catalog functions; a renderer without them rejects the call. The built-ins run only in the browser: the agent cannot call them with `callRendererFunction`.

On React Native, these run in the app, the same way, with two differences. `openUrl` fails with "openUrl is not available on this platform", reported like any failed function, because there is no `window.open`; to open a link there, declare a catalog function of your own whose handler calls `Linking.openURL`. And Hermes has no `Intl.PluralRules`, so `pluralize` picks its form with the English rule: `one` for 1 and -1, `other` for any other number (`zero` still applies to 0).

Both appear to the model as regular catalog functions; a renderer without them rejects the call. The built-ins run only in the browser (on React Native, in the app): the agent cannot call them with `callRendererFunction`.

`defineModel` reads the prop and emits `update:email` when the user types:

When the agent binds `email` to a value of the surface, what the user types is written there. From then on, that value belongs to the user: a later agent update cannot write over it. The agent still sees the value on its next run.

The data model keeps a copy of the value, made as `structuredClone` makes one, so a `Date`, a `Map`, a `Set`, `NaN` and `Infinity` stay as they are, and a class instance becomes a plain object. The agent reads the value from the JSON of the next request, so it sees what `JSON.stringify` makes of it: `NaN` and `Infinity` become `null`, a valid `Date` its ISO string (an invalid one `null`), and a `Map` or a `Set` `{}`. A value that JSON cannot hold (a bigint, or a value with a cycle) is still written, but the agent is not told it, and a warning is logged with `console.warn`. A value that `structuredClone` refuses (a function, a symbol, a `WeakMap`, a `Promise`) writes nothing, and the error goes to the generative UI `onError` (`errorBoundary.onError` in React and React Native) as a props failure. Setting `null` or `undefined` removes the value: the path still belongs to the user, so later agent writes to it are still ignored, and the agent sees it as `null`.
Now the card shows live cart data, its button runs your code, and the form keeps the user's input.
A **surface** is one piece of generated UI. Each surface renders in a **target**, a place where generated UI can go:
- **The chat.** Always there. The agent can use every component of the catalog.
- **A page target.** An area of your page that you mark with `GenerativeUISurface`, or `<copilot-generative-ui-surface>` in Angular. The agent sees it only while it is on screen.

- **The chat.** Always there. The agent can use every component of the catalog. On React Native, you draw chat surfaces yourself, with `GenerativeUIActivity`; see [Chat surfaces on React Native](#chat-surfaces-on-react-native). The agent is offered the chat target even when the app shows no chat, so a React Native app that renders only `GenerativeUISurface` targets, or only the prebuilt `CopilotChat` (which does not draw surfaces yet), never shows a surface aimed at the chat.
- **A page target.** An area of your page that you mark with `GenerativeUISurface`, or `<copilot-generative-ui-surface>` in Angular. The agent sees it only while it is mounted.
Wrap an area of your page in a target. Give it an id, and tell the agent what the area is for:
The content of the element is the fallback.
export function FeaturedProducts({ products }: { products: Product[] }) {

description="The Featured Products row of the home screen. When the customer asks to see products here, show them as a ProductGrid with one ProductCard for each product. When they ask for the featured products again, delete this surface."

`style` applies to the `View` around the surface, which also holds the fallback, so the spacing stays the same when the agent's row replaces yours. `GenerativeUISurface` throws when no `GenerativeUIProvider` is above it, and shows its fallback under a provider that has no `ui`. A target follows the thread that is active in the provider, the thread of the last run that started on the core (of any agent), so it suits a screen that shares its agent with the chat. To show the output of one particular agent, such as a background run that composes a home screen, render that agent's activity message with `GenerativeUIActivity`; see [Chat surfaces on React Native](#chat-surfaces-on-react-native).

description="The Featured Products row of the home page. When the customer asks to see products here, show them as a ProductGrid with one ProductCard for each product. When they ask for the featured products again, delete this surface."
The default slot is the fallback.
- `id`: the target id. The agent names it when it renders here.
- `description`: what the area is and what belongs in it. The agent reads it on every run, so write it like an instruction.
- `fallback`: shows until the agent renders here, and again after the agent deletes its surface. In Angular, the projected content is the fallback.
- `description`: what the area is and what belongs in it. The agent reads it in each run that starts while the target is mounted, so write it like an instruction.

- `fallback`: shows until the agent renders here, and again after the agent deletes its surface, unless an older surface of the same target and thread is still live: then that one shows. In Angular, the projected content is the fallback. In Vue, the default slot is the fallback.
- `ui` and `components`: the only components the agent can use here. See [Limit the components](#limit-the-components).
- The agent gets the list, so it knows what fits.
- An operation with another component is rejected, and the agent gets the reason.
- `ui` types the names, so a typo is a type error. Pass the same catalog that you gave the provider.
Leave out `components` (and `ui`) to allow every component of the catalog.

Leave out `components` (and `ui`) to allow every component of the catalog. Names that are not in the catalog are dropped, with a warning in development. An empty list, or one with only unknown names, allows no component: the target is still offered to the agent, but every operation that places a component in it is rejected.
When the agent starts to render into a target, the page scrolls to it, unless it is already on screen. Turn this off for one target:

React Native has no `autoScroll`. Instead, `onGenerationStart` is called once each time the agent starts to render into the target (each `render_ui` call, for a new surface or an update), and when the target mounts, its `id` changes, or the active thread changes, while the agent is rendering into it. A re-render, `<React.StrictMode>` or a new callback does not call it again for the same start, and an error it throws is caught and logged with `console.error`. A call counts as new when the surface starts streaming again, or keeps streaming while the runtime resets its rejected operations; so when a reconnect delivers the next call already streaming and neither call had a rejected operation, the two calls count as one start. Scroll there yourself. The position you have may be out of date when the call comes: a target that mounts while the agent renders into it gets the call before its first layout, and content above the target can move as the generation starts. So for a short time after each call, scroll again whenever `onLayout` gives a new position:
// Until this time, a new position of the target scrolls to it again.
// Undefined before the first layout: onLayout scrolls then.
{/* A direct child of the ScrollView, so its layout y is its offset in the content. */}
if (y === notesY.current) return; // same position: nothing to correct

On the web, with a sticky header, give surfaces some room at the top in your CSS:
A target can be specific. A product page can give each product its own target, so its recommendations stay with it when the user moves between products:
When the `id` input changes, the target is registered again under the new id, so no key is needed.
description={`The "You might also like" row under ${product.name}. Show related products here. Never include ${product.name} itself.`}
`The "You might also like" row under ${props.product.name}. Show related products here. Never include ${props.product.name} itself.`,
When the `id` prop changes, the target is registered again under the new id, so no `key` is needed.
Each component renders inside its own error boundary. One broken component shows a small fallback, and the rest of the surface keeps working. To report errors, or to draw your own fallback:

Angular has no per-component error boundary. A component that throws while it is created shows the fallback and reports to `onError`; an error in a later change detection goes to the `ErrorHandler` of the app. After a render error, the default fallback shows a Retry button that creates the component again with the current data. A custom `errorFallback` gets the same function in its `retry` input, if it declares one.

The default fallback is the `NodeFallback` of the provider's `host`, `NativeNodeFallback` unless you pass your own `host`: the error, in native views, and a Retry button after a render error. A component whose props fail its schema shows it too, with the reason and no Retry button; your own `fallback` is not used for it. When your `fallback` throws, the host fallback with Retry shows in its place; when the host fallback throws, the node renders nothing. Either way the failure stays in its node, and it is reported to `onError`.

There is no Inspector on React Native. `onError` gets render failures, invalid props, failed events, failed functions that a component called and the operations that the app rejected; a render failure or invalid props that stay the same while the agent sends new content are reported once, and a failed event or function on every call. Operations that the runtime rejected never reach `onError`. They reach the `rejected` and `error` props of the `Wrapper`: the `Wrapper` of `GenerativeUIActivity` for a chat surface, and the `Wrapper` of `GenerativeUISurface` for a surface in a named target. Both default wrappers show a short error line. The exception is a rejected `createSurface`. A named target then keeps its fallback and renders no `Wrapper`; when the app rejected it, `onError` gets it and `<GenerativeUIActivity target="<id>">` shows it. When the runtime rejected it, no activity message is sent for it, so only the model learns of it, in the result of its `render_ui` call, and nothing on the device shows it. The one exception is a `createSurface` with the id of a live surface: the runtime adds that rejection to the live surface, whose `Wrapper` shows it. See [Errors on the device](/ms-agent-harness-dotnet/react-native#errors-on-the-device).
The fallback is a Vue component. It gets `error`, `retry`, `surfaceId`, and `componentId` as props:
:generativeUI="{ ui: shopUI, errorBoundary: { onError, fallback: RetryFallback } }"
On every run, the agent gets:
- The targets that are on screen, with their descriptions and component limits.
- The targets that are mounted, with their descriptions and component limits, and the chat target.
- The surfaces that already exist, so it can update one in place instead of building a new one.
- The values the user typed into a surface. The agent cannot write over those values.
- The operations that the browser rejected, with the reason, so the agent can fix them.
- The operations that the runtime or the app (the browser, or the React Native app) rejected, with the reason, so the agent can fix them.

To see the same data, open the **Surfaces** tab of the Generative UI pane in Inspector. If a surface stays empty, see [When something does not render](/ms-agent-harness-dotnet/generative-ui/components#when-something-does-not-render).

lines.text: Every color, radius, shadow, and font of the standard components is a CSS variable. Set the variables with the `theme` option:
`theme` also takes a signal, which makes the theme reactive.
The binding is reactive. Keep `theme` in a `ref`, and the surfaces update when you change it.
The keys are typed. A name that the components do not read, such as `"--a2ui-color-acent"`, is a type error.

React Native has no standard catalog and no CSS variables, so its `GenerativeUIProvider` has no `theme` prop: passing one is a type error, and a `theme` passed from JavaScript, or through a cast, is dropped, with a warning in development. Style the components of your own catalog with `StyleSheet`, as you style the rest of your app. See [Generative UI with your own components](/ms-agent-harness-dotnet/react-native#generative-ui-with-your-own-components).
Your editor lists all of them when you type a key in `theme`. To type a theme in its own file, use `GenerativeUITheme`:
If your app already switches dark mode with a `dark` class, there is nothing to do. To follow the system setting, set the class with a small script in the `<head>`, so the page does not flash:
The agent must send the UI to the browser somehow. Some agents are good at tool calls. Others only stream text, or you build their prompt yourself. A **transport** is the way the UI travels:

The agent must send the UI to the app somehow: the browser, or a React Native app. Some agents are good at tool calls. Others only stream text, or you build their prompt yourself. A **transport** is the way the UI travels:
- **Tool** (the default): the agent calls a `render_ui` tool.
- **Markdown**: the agent writes the UI in `a2ui` code blocks inside its reply.
Both transports use the same catalogs, surfaces, and components. Only the path between the agent and the browser changes.
Both transports use the same catalogs, surfaces, and components. Only the path between the agent and the app changes.
| The agent writes UI | as `render_ui` tool calls | in `a2ui` code blocks in its reply |
| Checked before the browser gets it | yes, by the runtime, and again in the browser | in the browser |
| Checked before the app gets it | yes, by the runtime, and again in the app | in the app |
| Text around the UI | a separate message | the same reply, before and after the UI |
| Works with | agents that use the run's tools and context | any agent that streams text |
This is the default, so the provider needs only the catalog:
React Native always uses the tool transport. It has no `standardUI`, so `shopUI` stands for a catalog of your own native components.

When a run carries the catalog, the runtime adds the `render_ui` tool and a short guide on how to call it. The runtime checks every operation while it streams, and the browser renders the valid ones at once.

When a run carries the catalog, the runtime adds the `render_ui` tool and a short guide on how to call it. The runtime checks every operation while it streams, and the browser (on React Native, the app) renders the valid ones at once.
The runtime option `generativeUI` controls when the tool is added:

Not available on React Native yet. `GenerativeUIProvider` always uses the tool transport, and `transport: "markdown"` is a type error there. A transport passed from JavaScript, or through a cast, is dropped, with a warning in development.

The provider sends the component schemas and a writing guide as context, and the agent writes the UI in its reply. See [Markdown mode](/ms-agent-harness-dotnet/generative-ui/components/markdown-mode) for what the agent writes, how it streams, and how to build your own prompt.
By default every agent gets generative UI. To give it only to some of them, list their ids:
